# My Journey

I used to preach [Buddhist enlightenment](http://mindset.u-dont-exist.com/) a lot. Eventually I realized you can feel spiritually free and still feel like the same little kid underneath when an old wound gets touched. The old childhood stuff can keep running your life even while the spiritual part feels free. I came to think that most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get above some childhood pain or some part of themselves they don't want to meet. That's [spiritual bypassing](https://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/). Plenty of seekers and gurus do this too; I've written about the [Dalai Lama as one example](https://substack.com/@udontexist/note/c-245314772?r=5vdc6m).

The way I picture it is almost stupidly simple. Imagine you're broke and starving, and your baby is starving too. *Understandable*: there is no food. Then a food bank opens nearby and suddenly you've got lots of nutritious munchies. But you're eating all of it yourself while baby you is still starving. *Unforgivable.*

That's what it can be like when you find real love or freedom on a spiritual path but it never reaches the little kid in you. Nobody would knowingly leave a baby starving. The catch is that a lot of us don't really believe there is a baby us in there. Once I started to feel that he was actually there, it became obvious that some of the love I'd found needed to reach him too.

I don't think people bypass because they're stupid or crazy. They're doing what they've figured out so far. I did it too. Until a few years ago, the whole inner-child idea sounded pretty silly to me. Then direct experience made him feel real. Reparenting started to feel like I was healing something that was actually there instead of finding another way to escape above it.

If all you're ever doing is managing the hurt kid, therapy can turn into a whole life organized around the wound. Spirituality opened a much bigger horizon for me—what happiness and love could mean beyond the conditions of my life story.

Not everybody needs to go looking for that. Some people already have enough love and meaning for the life they want and aren't especially curious for more. Great. But if ordinary life and conditional love have always felt radically insufficient to you, the question of whether something deeper is possible can become very hard to ignore.

### Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away

If you still feel like a kid inside, anything that seems genuinely grown-up can feel like salvation. You may end up handing the adult role to whoever or whatever seems to know how life works.

That can even help for a while. Borrowed adulthood is letting someone help you do one grown-up thing you can't do for yourself yet. The trouble starts when they keep the role instead of helping you practice it.

A helper can see something you can't see and still be wrong about you. They can challenge you or show you what a steadier adult looks like without getting the last word over your life. Even [Pema Chödrön](https://pemachodronfoundation.org/product/taking-the-leap-book/), from a tradition where devotion to a teacher is a big deal, says the teacher should “wean us from dependency altogether” and help us grow up.

Spiritual practice can change how pain feels, but it can't do the adult task for you. If the problem is out in the world, it may need an outside action. If something in your actual life is unsafe, love for the child may mean getting out or getting practical help. A teaching that turns real danger into merely “your story” has stopped protecting the child.

If you grew up learning that what you wanted didn't matter, no-self teachings can land like a trap. You finally start trying to find out who you are, and somebody tells you there is no you. Maybe one day that teaching becomes freeing. First you may need enough of a self to stand somewhere. Otherwise “there is no self” can become a very sophisticated way of disappearing again.

Disagreement is not automatically resistance to healing. Sometimes the helper is simply wrong about you, or their method is trying to take you somewhere you don't want to go. A good helper can consider that without turning your objection into proof that you need more of their help.

The test I care about is whether I slowly need the helper less. If we disagree, I want to be able to stay on my own ground and make a sane decision without needing them to certify that I'm doing adulthood correctly.

Borrow adulthood. Do not surrender it. The right helper stands beside you for a while, teaches what they can, and gradually hands your life back.

My own version was strange. I was well-loved as a child, but from age twelve to twenty-six I was depressed and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. [Loving-kindness (metta) meditation](http://love.u-dont-exist.com/) healed that depression almost instantly for me.

The love was already there. My parents had given me a lot of it. I found more in [Buddhist teachings—which, it turns out, also include inner-child self-love!](https://substack.com/profile/355021294-u-dont-existcom/note/c-297324975) and later in [loveyhuasca](http://soma.u-dont-exist.com/). Metta gave all of that love somewhere to land.

But it didn't reach everything. A lot of the child stuff around my attachment to women was still there. When I later tried [self-directed inner-child therapy](https://youtu.be/yEWFjODXJbI?si=IXUqrhExojOm6Itm), it felt imaginary at first. I used San Pedro cactus and also CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, and that cracked it open; structured sessions with an inner-child therapist deepened it.

That's how the method grew beyond “find the wounded child and love them.” The adult still has to do the three jobs from the map. But protective parts can stand in the doorway, and sometimes you can't feel like the adult at all. Borrowed adulthood is what I was missing for that last problem.
